We have analysed the asymmetry of lineshapes in spectral patterns to identify the presence of quadratic anisotropy in an exotic $B_s^0\to D_s^{*-} \mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ decay, a indication of a specific type of differential variation that characterizes local anisotropy in a highly excited, quark-gluon plasma. By applying a angle-dependent asymmetry study to this decay, we can gather information about the direction of motion and the angle between the decay products. Although a thorough understanding of the underlying processes calls for sophisticated simulations, a simplified approach utilizing a angular coefficient ratio allows for the extraction of a quark-gluon plasma plasma momentum distribution given by $e^{\frac{E_T}{T_{\text{eff}}}}\frac{1}{4\pi T_{\text{eff}}^2}\frac{1-\frac{E_T}{T_{\text{eff}}}}{1+\frac{E_T}{T_{\text{eff}}}}$, where $E_T$ and $T_{\text{eff}}$ are measures of the energy and effective temperature of the plasma, respectively. This result demonstrates that lineshape asymmetry can be a sensitive indicator of quadratic anisotropy in the plasma, and could be confirmed with a total of 60 times more $B_s^0$ decay data than currently available. Additionally, with 100 times more data, lineshape asymmetry may be measurable in other decay channels. An analysis of the decay $B_s^0\to \eta' \rho^0$ is also presented, and indicates that the anisotropy in this decay is 1.5 times larger than that of $B_s^0\to \phi \rho^0$, and has a different spectral shape that could be distinguished with 10 times more data than currently available. An analysis of the decay $B_s^0\to K^* \bar{K}^{*0}$ is also provided, and shows that the anisotropy in this decay is similar to that of $B_s^0\to \phi \rho^0$, and has a larger branching fraction than previously estimated. Furthermore, we have also derived constraints on the anisotropy in other decay channels, and have identified candidates for future sensitivity to lineshape asymmetry in exotic charmed and bottomed decays.   question remains regarding the optimal structure of RNN, particularly in terms
  of whether to utilize feedback loops for input information. We challenge the
  widespread assumption that RNN models necessarily incorporate past input, a
  concept we call "input loop assumption." Through careful analysis and subsequent
  experimentation with large datasets, our findings reveal that the input loop
  assumption is, in fact, unnecessary and even detrimental in many instances. As
  we demonstrate, removing the input loop from basic RNN models leads to
  superior performance in various benchmark tasks, including language understanding
  and generation tasks, as well as the classification of visual data. Our research
  shows that removing the input loop simply allows the model to learn more complex
  representations from the feedback loop, a component that has been underestimated
  in its capabilities. We hope this understanding will guide future RNN model
  developments and highlight the potential of the feedback loop as a standalone
  feature extractor. As evidence of the broad applicability of this concept, we
  successfully incorporate the feedback loop into a vision transformer model, a
  step we believe marks the first instance of doing so, and find this modification
  to be particularly beneficial in tasks that place a high premium on contextual
  understanding. As supported by our findings, simply using the feedback loop

  relationships and has the added benefit of reducing the reliance on massive
  parameterizations, a phenomenon we term "loop knowledge". This newly identified
  mechanism of learning from the feedback loop has significant implications for the
  design of large-scale transformer models and highlights the critical role that
  the input loop assumption plays in limiting the capabilities of RNN models. As

for tasks such as navigation and sports requires significant positioning precision.  To meet this need, a model is proposed for online estimation of a robot's actual position compared to its intended path, taking into account factors such as wheel slippage.  This comparison, referred to as latency, is then utilized in a controller algorithm to ensure the robot remains within a safe distance from obstacles.  The proposed method, latency-aware motion control, leverages a simple simulation model and feedback from wheel rotation speeds to estimate latency.  This estimation, in turn, helps to identify and prevent wheel slippage.  The proposed system was implemented on a racing robot and the results show that simple model-based estimation of latency leads to effective control of robot speed and staying close to planned path.  In particular, it outperforms a comparable, more complex model-based estimation method in terms of speed and precision.  The proposed motion control algorithm has been tested on a real robot and the data indicates a successful combination of high speed, accurate path-following and minimal wheel slippage. The code for the proposed method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/shah89/LMC. As the hadronic lepton jet criteria becomes more selective, we find that cross-sections decrease rapidly due to the exclusion of hard leptons. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of two extrapolation methods to extend cross-section measurements to more restrictive lepton jet definitions. By extrapolating to more selective definitions, we derive estimates for minimal cross-section values within 5 standard deviations of detection limits, which we report for various definitions of lepton jets incorporating electrons and muons. We also explore cross-sections for more exclusive scenarios where events feature either electrons alone or muons alone within the accepted kinematic range. As the rejection power of lepton jet discrimination improves, we observe a significant decrease in cross-sections, and for the most extreme case of muon jets with high transverse momentum, we find little overlap with the phase space defined by initial criteria, suggesting further refinement in the algorithm may be beneficial. This research enriches our understanding of hadronic lepton jet cross-sections in high-energy collisions and provides a solid basis for identifying signs of new physics emerging as rare leptonic events. This is the second part of a study presented in arXiv:2106.09033, which focused on theoretical aspects and cross-section predictions for hadronic lepton jets. Based on lattice QCD outcomes and Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model estimates, we previously estimated the magnitude of rare leptonic processes, such as the vacuum decay into leptons and two photons, within the hadronic lepton jet framework. In this part, we outline our experimental approach, describe the identification of hadronic lepton jets using a machine learning-based algorithm, and present comprehensive measurements of cross-sections for various definitions of hadronic lepton jets across a wide range of transverse momenta. This study was possible due to the large sample size of 64 pb$^{-1}$ of lattice QCD-inspired fake data recorded by the PHENIX experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). growing interest in using machine learning models for forecasting extreme events such as tropical cyclones, droughts, and heatwaves. However, creating and evaluating machine learning models for predicting rare events is particularly challenging due to their inherent difficulty and the resulting models which often tend to overestimate the frequency of extreme events. Additionally, accessing data from weather satellites and model simulations is typically restricted and requires collaboration with research institutions and organizations. Furthermore, securing access to supercomputers for conducting large-scale experiments using weather models is commonly necessary but often limiting. This research project focuses on making historical satellite imagery and weather model data accessible, and it introduces an open-source tool for easily training machine learning models using these datasets. This tool addresses the difficulties mentioned above by providing free access to data and simplifying the development of machine learning models for predicting extreme weather events. To demonstrate the capabilities of this tool, we have trained three different machine learning models using historical data from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-5P satellite and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' IAMAP9.0 weather model, and we have used these models to make forecasts for future events. This has allowed us to recover about 75% of actual extreme events from satellite and weather model data, and we have further validated these results using weather stations and surface pressure sensors in the Maldives and the Caribbean. This research also includes an analysis of performance evaluation metrics and a discussion of potential issues with satellite and weather model data that can lead to the detection of non-extreme events. This project has made open-source code and data available at https://github.com/ExtremesWeather.

This guide focuses on the mathematical representation of spacetime's flexible nature in relation to a point mass object using Einstein's General Theory of Relativity. We will derive the gravitational redshift phenomenon, a phenomenon also predicted by Einstein's gravitational field equations, using a non-absolute spacetime approach. This non-relativistic, non-conservative gravity framework, first proposed by Einstein in 1922, will be applied to derive the mass-momentum relationship and Keplerian motion of a point mass object in orbit. This section of the guide covers the historical basis for Einstein's original derivate of the mass-momentum relationship and Keplerian motion, often referred to as the "pre-relativistic" or "non-relativistic" derivation of Kepler's laws. We will also examine the mathematical similarities between Einstein's original derivations and those achieved through the conservation of four-momentum in special relativity, in addition to the conservation of the angular momentum tensor in spin-2 gravity. This guide aims to critically examine the historical basis for Einstein's original derivations of the mass-momentum relationship and Keplerian motion, and to explore the applicability of modern gravity theories to a point mass object in motion. As such, it is primarily directed towards researchers in the fields of physics and the history of science. This guide assumes a high-school level understanding of classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and special relativity, in addition to a basic knowledge of differential geometry and the Einstein field equations. As such, it includes an introductory appendix on the fundamentals of differential geometry, the Einstein field equations, and the Einstein stress-energy tensor. This guide is organized into sections that correspond to the historical progression of Einstein's work, from his early preoccupation with the nature of gravity to his later focus on the gravitational influence on the curvature of spacetime. VLBI data and estimate the accuracy required to determine the Galaxies 
Grouping parameter and mass of galaxy clusters. A thorough examination of 
existing observations led to the identification of suitable target active 
galactic nuclei. We discuss the results of repeated measurements for the 
M87* object, analyze possible sources of measurement uncertainty, and 
examine the feasibility of measuring the motion of galaxy clusters with a 
high degree of precision using radio waves emitted by active galactic nuclei. 

We highlight potential synergies between this experiment and other large-scale 
galaxy structure research projects, present the proposed observations schedule 
for the M87* object, and outline the necessary steps to achieve the desired 
accuracy in measuring the motion of galaxy clusters based on VLBI data. 

We discuss the implications of measuring the motion of galaxy clusters on the 
Galaxies Grouping parameter and mass scales for galaxy clusters, and examine 
the potential to refine the Galaxies Grouping parameter and mass estimates of 
galaxy clusters by conducting more accurate measurements of galaxy cluster 
motion using VLBI technique.

  angular momentum impacts the formation of stellar clusters, particularly in 
  highly turbulent environments. To achieve this, we conducted extensive, 
  two-dimensional SPH simulations of molecular cloud collapse, under various 
  levels of turbulence. Following this, we analyzed the resulting cluster 
  properties, focusing on angular momentum's effects in comparison to those of 
  turbulence. To further investigate these findings, we refined our simulations 
  to study the influence of both internal and external factors on cluster 
  formation, considering factors like gas clumps, angular momentum, and 
  turbulence. 

  Methods. We utilized a high-resolution, multi-dimensional core-accretion 
  model to simulate the formation of individual stars and their subsequent 
  interaction with their surroundings. This model allowed us to accurately 
  model the effects of both stellar feedback and angular momentum. We then 
  analyzed our results to better understand how angular momentum influences 
  cluster formation in turbulent environments. To this end, we conducted 
  in-depth analyses of both simulated cluster formations and individual star 
  formations. 

  Results. Our findings indicate that the distribution of angular momentum 
  among molecular clouds significantly impacts the resulting cluster properties, 
  with far-reaching effects on the formation of individual stars. When the 
  distribution of angular momentum is uniform, we observe the formation of 
  massive clusters with a wide mass range, along with a notable presence of 
  low-mass stars. In contrast, areas with high concentrations of angular 
  momentum tend to form massive stars at their cores. Additionally, we found 
  that the presence of massive clouds with uniform angular momentum can lead 
  to the formation of star clusters with significant mass disparities, along 
  with the creation of massive stars that get dispersed due to too much 
  repulsive pressure. We attribute this to the redistribution of angular 
  momentum via stellar feedback. 

  Discussion. Our simulations reveal that the effects of angular momentum on 
  cluster formation are just as significant as those of turbulence. We propose 
  that the distribution of angular momentum among molecular clouds should be 
  considered a crucial factor when explaining the formation of massive star 
  clusters, along with the presence of gas clumps that occur as a result of 
  cloud fragmentation. We further suggest that the distribution of angular 
  momentum among these clumps determines the resulting cluster properties, 
  including its mass, degree of scattering, and the presence of low-mass 
  stars.

Initially, VWE breaks down navigation direction sequences into their numerical equivalent values, then uses a custom encoding method to convert these values into compressed binary formats.  To evaluate the effectiveness of VWE, we applied it to an extensive dataset of 1.8 million OSMPediance files and measured the resulting compression ratios, finding them to be impressively low, at around 0.36% when using the adaptive encoding approach and an even more minuscule 0.23% when using the non-adaptive method.  To assess VWE's computational efficiency, we measured its decoding and encoding times for the same large dataset of navigation data sequences and found them to be exceedingly fast, taking only 0.37 seconds to decode and 0.29 seconds to encode an average OSMPediance file.  To further explore VWE's applicability, we experimented with using its compressed binary representations as input for existing navigation data analysis tasks and found that it can be used as a drop-in replacement for the original data, producing nearly identical results.  To improve VWE, we experimented with alternative encoding methods and found that using a probability distribution that takes into account the surrounding direction values significantly enhances its performance.  Finally, we demonstrated VWE's versatility by incorporating it into an end-to-end OSMTile compression pipeline, which we call Vial Compression, and evaluated its performance on a large dataset of tiles, finding it to be remarkably effective, achieving compression ratios of up to 3.3% while maintaining an exceptionally low computational overhead of 0.6 seconds per tile. By combining 137 fb-2 of proton-proton collision data collected at 13 TeV by the ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments, we conduct a joint measurement of the top pair production cross-section and top quark mass in this region.  Due to the limited number of candidate events with top quarks decaying into bottom quarks, we utilize a combination of candidates with at least one misidentified b jet.  The measured cross-section for saturated events with at least one misidentified b jet is 93 pb ± 10 pb, and we calculate the average top quark mass using the threshold fit method as 173.9 GeV ± 2.8 GeV, based on a combination of candidates with top quarks detected through their leptonic decays.  We further explore the behavior of the cross-section in the 1.2 to 1.5 TeV range and find that it aligns with the prediction of the next-to-leading order QCD theory.  Additionally, we employ machine learning algorithms to improve the identification efficiency of b jets and observe a boost in efficiency of up to 20% over traditional baseline methods.  This research marks the first instance of a collaborative effort among all three main LHC experiments for a physics analysis.  We have made this research accessible for various audiences through an engaging narrative and simplified mathematical presentations of key concepts.  This study paves the way for a unified front in extracting valuable information from the LHC data, and encourages further collaborative work among the experiments on top quark-related topics. Our analysis reveals that the magnetic field can hinder the phantom energy's negative impact, potentially leading it to contribute positively to the universe's expansion. As modern systems continually evolve to handle larger datasets efficiently, the importance of memory efficiency in machine learning has become a critical factor. A common technique used to achieve efficient memory usage involves interconnecting multiple cards to increase memory capacity while speeding up computations. However, using many cards complicates memory management due to significant communication costs between cards. In an effort to simplify memory management and optimize performance, this research proposes an innovative memory efficient GPU memory manager called TinyMap. TinyMap is particularly effective at minimizing memory allocation delays and improving memory utilization when using a large number of cards. Experimental results show that TinyMap delivers significant improvements in performance and reduced memory allocation delays. In particular, using TinyMap on 64 cards leads to a peak performance of 1.68 times that of the industry-standard memory manager, while also cutting memory allocation delays to 0.45 seconds from 5 seconds.  Experimental data and a sample code are available at \url{https://github.com/ChengNei/TinyMap}.  We hope that TinyMap will serve as a solid starting point for developing high-performance, memory-efficient GPU memory managers. Nonlinear noise enhancement occurs when the average photon number exceeds a certain threshold, and it dominates all other sources of photon loss in the quantum regime.  This study investigates the impact of nonlinear noise enhancement on squeezed light transmitted through a fiber, and it demonstrates that it can destroy all the quantum advantage that squeezing provides over classical methods in many instances.  Additionally, it indicates the minimum loss threshold beyond which the teleportation of squeezed states via fiber becomes less efficient than classical amplification.  Based on numerical calculations, we derive an analytical expression for the photon number of the nonlinear noise spectrum, and we utilize this result to estimate the minimum requirements for successful teleportation of squeezed states via fiber.  These conditions include satisfying the photon-number threshold, meeting the coherence threshold, and ensuring that the photon number of the nonlinear noise spectrum is substantially lower than the average photon number.  If these conditions are not met, the communication protocol becomes less efficient than classical amplification, and the reduction in success probability is significant for small values of the average photon number.  Therefore, it is crucial to choose parameters that minimize the photon number of the nonlinear noise spectrum as much as possible, and to seek solutions that move beyond the quantum regime.   To capitalize on this spectrum, researchers have focused on enhancing spatial reuse through multi-user mmWave networking, often incorporating massive arrays.
  However, the inherent limitations of array systems create restrictions on spatial reuse, particularly from neighboring cells, which could interfere heavily.
  In fact, this interference can resemble a "shaped beam" and provide a new form of throughput for nearby users, which we refer to as "sideband" throughput.
  In this research, we identify sideband throughput as a hidden benefit of array-based mmWave networking and measure its presence and potential.
  We introduce an energy detection method to locate sidebands, which involves analyzing the signal power across scanned directions.
  In particular, we propose a Spatial-Sideband Detection (SSD) algorithm that selects the most promising directions and evaluates the corresponding sideband throughput with a metric we call the Sideband Detection Value (SDV).

This research focuses on a specific extension called quasi-metric spaces, which we rebrand as QM-spaces. This rebranding helps avoid confusion with existing definitions of quasi-metric spaces. This paper reviews the fundamentals of QM-spaces and goes on to explore recently developed concepts within the field, including fixed point results for QM-spaces and their applications to nonlinear dynamics. A new theorem is proven here: if a QM-space has the property of being complete and if a non-decreasing sequence within that space is defined, then the limit of that sequence can be determined. This result has the potential to impact the study of population dynamics, a nonlinear system of equations. A brief overview of the Brinkhoff dataset and Dynkin's theorem on metric spaces is also provided. This research is an extension of ideas discussed at the International Conference on Nonlinear Analysis and Applications held in Hail, Saudi Arabia. As a particle moves through this design, changes in the optical field's grating affect the phase shift it incurs, resulting in a spatially-modulated phase response that can be used to represent a discrete Fourier transform matrix. As a result, any input field particle will be steered to a specific output position based on its initial frequency. As demonstrated in Figure 1, this concept can be extended to control the direction of light fields with multiple frequencies and understand the behavior of a 2D photonic crystal coupled resonator array. As shown in Section 2, this design can be modified to include branching channels and delay lines. A working model of this design has been fabricated and tested, as presented in Section 4. Finally, as shown in Section 5, this design can be expanded to handle multi-frequency field particles and a larger spectral range. The development of this phase filter is notable for its small size, precise control over light field particles, and the automated sorting of light fields based on their frequency. As a result, this design has significant potential for use in micro-photonical component arrays, artificial compound eyes, and zero-index photonic devices. ological implications of a recently proposed extension to the Standard Model known as the "Universal Vector Multiplet Dominance" scenario, which incorporates a specific principle that vectors behave as the most dominant particles in all interactions. We examine concrete physical predictions made possible by this phenomenon within the UVMD framework and focus on the electroweak sector. Calculating the one-loop corrections to the Higgs boson decay into $W^+W^-$, we derive a precise deviation from the nominal QCD-like SM prediction, given by $(\Delta R_{WW})_{\rm UVMD} = 0.239$. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of this phenomenon on existing and future Higgs boson experiments at the LHC, identifying observable effects on Higgs boson production and its main decay channels, particularly $WW \to HH$. Consequently, we propose a straightforward strategy to test this prediction through focused measurements of Higgs boson decays into $WW$ or $ZZ$ or the search for $HH \to (b \bar b)(\tau^-\tau^+)$. Additionally, we emphasize the potential of future experiments at the 100 TeV collider to confidently verify the UVMD scenario through more stringent probes of Higgs boson production and its rare decay modes, which could lead to a deeper understanding of this phenomenon and its roots.   Considering the growing quantity of mobile applications and resulting data, there's a
  growing need to speed up access to these services without compromising security.
  Head-to-head wireless networking allows devices to connect directly to each other, 
  potentially enhancing data transfer speeds, all while maintaining robust security.

  head wireless networking to create a faster, more secure connection to cloud services
  using a mobile device's nearby peers. We collected detailed data on transfer speeds

  be significantly accelerated, all while maintaining robust security.

of the Gumbel-maximum trick, a
  crucial algorithm in statistical modeling that assigns discrete labels based on
  Gumbel-distributed log-likelihood values. Although the trick's efficacy has
  been demonstrated through successful implementations, the underlying theory to
  govern its performance remains poorly understood. Specifically, we lack a clear
  understanding of the algorithm's robustness in the presence of scarce data.
  Our research addresses this ignorance by establishing expected and
  asymptotic performance benchmarks for the Gumbel-maximum trick in various
  settings, including situations with abundant and limited data. The results
  indicate that the algorithm's performance can be unstable when relying on
  randomized decisions, and we connect this instability to the presence of
  modes in the underlying probability distribution. To mitigate this issue, we
  leverage a common regulatory requirement called the strict saddle
  condition, previously introduced in neural network contexts. Our findings
  confirm that the algorithm's performance becomes significantly more robust
  when the strict saddle condition is satisfied, even with limited data. 
  Our research also highlights the importance of exploring randomized saddle
  points in the optimization process. To accommodate this discovery, we
  introduce a new version of the stochastic Gumbel-maximum trick algorithm
  that balances randomized and deterministic draws based on data quality. 
  Our empirical evaluations validate the algorithm's performance in various
  tasks and provide valuable insights into the optimal design of the algorithm
  components. The code for the experiments is available at
  \url{https://github.com/ShenLiaoRegret/tree/sota/SNGUMMAX}. 
  This paper also includes an initial result on the asymptotic convergence
  rate of the Gumbel-maximum trick, which we believe is a starting point
  for further theoretical investigations. 
  Our approach to developing the stochastic Gumbel-maximum trick relies on
  an innovative application of the rejection sampling method in conjunction
  with the randomized search dynamic. Our research paves the way for more
  rigorous analysis of the algorithm's asymptotic behavior and encourages
  further development of theory to support the widespread adoption of the
  Gumbel-maximum trick in statistical modeling. 
  We hope that our work sparks a surge in theoretical investigations of the
  Gumbel-maximum trick and related algorithms, which we believe is critical
  for overcoming the limitations imposed by the current lack of robustness
  benchmarks.

detected the first hint of lepton-flavour non-uniformity in tau-lepton pair production in $e^+e^-$ collisions, based on 11 days of data collected at $\sqrt{s} \approx 182.7$ GeV. With an integrated luminosity of 260 pb$^{-1}$, the experiment reported a signal for tau-pair production with a significance of 3.5 standard deviations, compared to the 1 standard deviation expected in scenarios with lepton flavours. The result also extends the knowledge of Drell-Yan tau-pair production at the energy level of 180 GeV. Furthermore, the experiment extracted precise measurements of the cross-section for this process, allowing for calculations of forward scattering amplitudes and the study of the ratio of helicity non-conservation. The findings also supported the presence of the $Z$ boson resonance and facilitated measurements of its properties. The discovered signal could potentially be associated with the violation of lepton flavour universality and marks a key area for investigation in future experiments. The research was conducted by the AS$\gamma$ collaboration and involves scientists from China, Russia, and the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). The study was published in an article titled "First Evidence of Tau Lepton Pair Production in $e^+e^-$ Collisions" and presented at the 2022 Lepton-Photon Conference. The preprint is available on the arXiv server under the ID number 2206.01878. The research was supported by grants from the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Alexander Bocharov Research Foundation, the Russian Science Foundation, and the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Russian Federation. The experiment was conducted using the Tibet-III detector at the Daya Bay site in Shangluo, China. The researchers employed a novel multivariate analysis technique that combines information from calorimetry and magnetic field measurements to identify tau leptons. The analysis involved selecting events with high energy deposits and significant magnetic field deflections, excluding events with electron or muon signatures. The researchers also implemented a multivariate machine learning model to distinguish tau-pair events from background events. The analysis was challenging due to the limited understanding of hadronization in tau decays and the limited efficiency of tau particle identification. The researchers addressed these issues by incorporating additional variables into the machine learning model and validating the analysis with simulated data. The analysis indicated that the Tibet-III detector has the capability to identify tau leptons with high efficiency and purity.

Utilizing tractography data from diffusion MRI, a group of researchers created an accurate map of the brain's structural connections and explored the intricate geometry of the DMN in individuals with schizophrenia and healthy controls. Our study applied a novel graph-based analysis method to reconstruct the brain's connectivity and created a standardized atlas of the DMN based on its intrinsic organization. To further investigate the default mode network's architecture, we used measures of graph theory to analyze connections within the DMN and between it and other brain networks. Our results showed that the default mode network has a distinct, globally uniform tendency to integrate information and maintain segregated identities, which could be crucial aspects of its functioning. However, individuals with schizophrenia had altered default mode network architecture characterized by an increased tendency to blend information and difficulties in maintaining boundaries, which was correlated with their reduced working memory capacity. Our findings also revealed that changes in the default mode network's architecture are specific to schizophrenia and are not observed in individuals with bipolar disorder. This study provides a novel, biologically-plausible explanation for the cognitive difficulties experienced by individuals with schizophrenia, including problems with memory. Further research is needed to explore the developmental pathways underlying these changes and the role of childhood trauma in modifying the brain's connectivity. By applying this method to LHC data, specifically proton-proton collision events collected at 13 TeV energies, we investigated processes featuring two muons and missing energy. By analyzing these processes from the perspective of effective theory, we were able to derive a key process into a dimension-reduced form, which we then incorporated into a likelihood function for our statistical analysis. By utilizing a combination of existing LHC data and theoretical knowledge, we were able to set a range of limits on the coefficient of the effective operator in question, specifically for the process involving two muons and missing energy. Based on this, we found that certain processes involving two muons and missing energy at the LHC may already be sensitive to new physics beyond the Standard Model at scales as high as 3 TeV. As such, we believe that effective field theory will continue to serve as a reliable tool for the exploration of lepton-flavour non-universality at the LHC, which in turn may lead to a deeper understanding of the underlying neutrino physics. In addition, effective field theory facilitates the conversion of results from the effective description back to the underlying theory, which is crucial for the interpretation of future direct and indirect searches for the new physics responsible for lepton-flavour non-universality.   The $k$-th power of an undirected graph $\G$ is defined as the undirected graph whose edges are formed from the edges in $\G$, using the rule that two vertices in $\G$ can form an edge in the power if they are connected by at least $k$ edges.

  A subhypergraph $\hat{\H}$ of a subhypergraph $\hat{\G}$ of an undirected graph $\G$ means that every edge in $\hat{\H}$ is also an edge in $\hat{\G}$.

  The number of edges in the $k$-th power of an undirected graph $\G$ is denoted as $e_\G^k$.

  For a subhypergraph $\hat{\H}$ of the $k$-th power of an undirected graph $\G$, the coverage ratio of $\hat{\H}$ is given by the formula $\rho(\hat{\H}) = \frac{\number\,of\, edges\, in\, \hat{\H}}{\number\,of\, edges\, in\, \G^k}$, denoted as $\rho(\hat{\H}) = \frac{e(\hat{\H})}{e_\G^k}$.

This study focuses on addressing the issue of finite-time contamination occurring when a component fails, and it aims to develop a state-feedback controller that can ensure the system remains stable and meets specific boundedness requirements, even if a component fails after some time. A key aspect is the incorporation of a component failure model that can cause finite-time contamination, and it is assumed that the component failure time is uncertain but has an upper limit.   Research has shown that listeners identify and recall themes in music
  through a process similar to pattern recognition, where a familiar shape
  is detected within a larger pattern. This process is made more difficult
  when musical themes are modified, such as through transposition, as seen
  in the varied reappearances of the "Dies Irae" melody throughout
  history. This challenge is also evident in the recollection of characters
  in social networks, where altered profile pictures can make users struggle
  to recognize and remember them. To better understand this process, we
  created a new task that involves detecting repeated musical motifs, even
  when they are transformed, and we conducted experiments using this task
  to study the role of memory in this process. Our findings revealed that
  pre-existing associations with a motif's meaning impede its recognition
  when it is modified, and we discovered that a threshold exists beyond
  which increased disfigurement makes recognition more difficult. We also
  found that repeated elements within a music piece, such as refrain
  melodies, are more easily recognized when more of the element is heard.

  Although machine learning provides valuable tools for analyzing existing data,
  using it to recommend personalized policies tailored to individual data sets
  remains a significant challenge due to missing target outputs and unestablished
  performance metrics for policy recommendations.
  With a focus on high-stakes policy decisions, this work develops a new
  framework for validating the effectiveness of policy learning from personalized
  recommendations.
  First, we introduce a theoretical foundation for assessing policy learning
  performance, based on the concept of expected outcome equilibrium, which
  considers the potential consequences of recommended policies in real-world
  scenarios.
  Then, we demonstrate that expected outcome equilibrium provides a legitimate
  performance metric for policy learning, given certain assumptions about the
  data and target outputs.
  Next, we develop data-driven methods for estimating the expected outcome
  equilibrium of policy learning from personalized recommendations.
  Finally, we apply this framework to evaluate the performance of policy learning
  in real-world settings, using administrative data from the state of New York
  to analyze the effects of personalized unemployment counseling on employment
  outcomes.
  The results show that policy learning from personalized recommendations leads
  to better employment outcomes, reducing the probability of losing a job and
  increasing the chance of finding a new job within a month.
  Furthermore, we find that policy learning from personalized recommendations
  results in higher overall employment, reduces the likelihood of quitting a
  job, and boosts the likelihood of taking on more work hours.
  The analysis also reveals that policy learning from personalized recommendations
  is cost-effective, covering the implementation expenses and yielding a
  significant return on investment.
  The findings support investing in policy learning from personalized
  recommendations to guide welfare programs and reduce unemployment.
  The code for evaluating policy learning performance using expected outcome
  equilibrium is publicly available at https://github.com/shiyion/policy_performance. Our analysis shows that the decay of quantum purity can be accurately described by a classical stochastic process, and we derive explicit expressions to relate the parameters of this process to the physical properties of the system and its environment. By simulating a quantum drum illuminated by a chaotic light source, our model demonstrates the emergence of a universal stochastic dynamics that reflects the system's interaction with the surrounding light field. Our findings also highlight how the purity decay rate is influenced by the strength of driving, and we identify a nonlinear relationship governing the decay of quantum antiphase phases. Our theoretical framework is applicable to a broad range of scenarios, including the dissipative dynamics of magnons in antiferromagnetic materials and the dynamics of quantum phases in driven-dissipative boson models. Our model has a key advantage over traditional approaches by allowing for the characterization of the dissipative dynamics from the knowledge of the initial state alone, a crucial insight that is demonstrated through the analysis of a quantum drum driven by a coherent light source. We further show that in certain scenarios, the purity decay can be minimized by optimizing the coherence of the driving process. Our results show that the number of prime powers of a specific modulus that fall within a given interval typically remains relatively small, exceeding a threshold of $\delta N$ only for a limited fraction of the prime powers, even when the interval in question is relatively large. In particular, we find that among the integers from 1 to N, the majority (greater than $1-\delta$) have a prime power modulus of at most $\text{Polylog}(N,\delta)$, and among the prime powers within this range, those with a modulus greater than $N^{1-\epsilon}$ are exceptionally rare, occurring less than $\delta N$ times. This research builds upon the framework established by the work of Banks, Harris, and Shuster, and it incorporates new insights gained from their result that the number of prime powers among dense subsets of the interval $[1, N]$ typically remains relatively small. This finding has implications for our understanding of the distribution of dense subsets of the interval $[1, N]$ and it leads to a stronger version of the well-known polynomial conjecture. This stronger conjecture posits that the number of polynomials of degree at most d with integer coefficients that identify a dense subset of the integers from 1 to N is essentially determined by the number of such polynomials with roots rather than the total number of possible polynomials. This stronger version of the polynomial conjecture is a more refined statement than its original counterpart and it is a crucial component in our proof of the result that the majority of the integers from 1 to N have a prime power modulus of at most $\text{Polylog}(N,\delta)$. Despite significant progress in graph-based methods, many real-world datasets lack properly labeled data, making graph sketching an increasingly vital technique.  However, current graph sketching research primarily focuses on supervised learning, neglecting the potential of unsupervised and semi-supervised learning.  In this paper, we introduce a new category of graph sketching techniques that leverages unsupervised and semi-supervised self-supervised learning frameworks to enhance graph-based machine learning models.  We propose an end-to-end unsupervised graph sketching framework, called Node Sketching AutoEncoder (NSAE), which employs a modular architecture to generate node labels from node embeddings through a decoding process similar to that used in vanilla AutoEncoders.  We further develop a semi-supervised version of NSAE, which incorporates a multi-task decoding process that combines node label prediction tasks.  Our experimental results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of NSAE in semi-contractive graph-based machine learning models, including Graph AutoEncoder (GAE) and SelfSupervised Graph Neural Networks (SSGNN).  Specifically, NSAE outperforms supervised and unsupervised baselines in node classification tasks, showing that our proposed framework enhances the representation learning capabilities of graph-based methods.  We also find that NSAE can adapt to new datasets through fine-tuning, demonstrating its transfer learning potential.  Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/NodeSketchingAutoEncoder.  We hope this work encourages further research in self-supervised graph sketching and provides a solid foundation for future studies.  In particular, exploring different self-supervised learning techniques and evaluating the performance of NSAE in other scenarios are recommended.  We also propose an evaluation metric for graph sketching techniques that utilizes the contractive loss incurred during training.  This metric detects situations in which the contractive loss is not effective, such as when NSAE fails to capture important node label information.  We further discover that NSAE may overlook crucial information when relying solely on the reconstruction loss during training.  To address this issue, we suggest incorporating additional supervision signals, such as the contractive loss, to guide the learning process of graph-based methods.  We also propose discarding the decoding process's early stages, which produce little informative node embeddings, to focus on extracting more representative features from the intermediate stages.   of MPEG-2 video compression, allowing efficient compression through 
  predictive encoding. However, the limitation on p-frame spacing significantly 
  hampers compression efficiency. This study proposes an innovative approach to 
  dynamically adjust p-frame spacing based on motion activity levels, which 
  are identified within local regions of the video frame. The proposed method, 
  known as Dynamic P-Frame Distance (DPFD), utilizes spatial motion analysis 
  to determine p-frame spacing. It prioritizes closer p-frame spacing in areas 
  exhibiting higher motion activity, thereby maintaining seamless video playback 
  and minimizing compression loss due to p-frame delay. Experimental results 
  indicate that DPFD outperforms conventional p-frame spacing strategies, 
  yielding significant Bit Rate (BR) savings of approximately 23.6% at the 
  Q0 quality level and 14.5% at the average BR in the JMVM codec scenario.

  larger p-frame spacings, showcasing its versatility and efficacy. This study 
  provides detailed, quantifiable assessment of DPFD's BR savings in relation 
  to varying p-frame spacings, p-frame spacing limits, and quantization 
  parameters, in addition to analyzing its computational overhead and 
  implementation complexity. This research focuses on the DPFD approach and 
  explores its potential applications in advanced video compression frameworks,

surrounding vehicles is crucial for drivers, 
  particularly in low-speed environments where there is little visibility. 
  Modern vehicles are equipped with multiple cameras providing a wide field of view, 
  yet these cameras have limited range and are affected by weather conditions. 
  To complement this data and enhance visibility, vehicles are also equipped with 
  short-range radar and ultrasonic sensors that measure distances from objects. 
  These sensors have limited angular viewbands and short detection ranges. 
  To integrate information across these sensors and enhance visibility, this paper 
  proposes a 3D vehicle motion forecasting model that utilizes multi-sensor data 
  and guides forecasted vehicles towards areas with minimal line-of-sight from 
  cameras. 
  Experimental results on a large real-world driving dataset show that this model 
  performs better than existing methods and simpler spatial embedding baselines. 
  This improvement holds when evaluated using rigorous driving scenarios with 
  limited camera visibility. 
  The proposed approach also facilitates the creation of training and test scenes 
  without collision between vehicles. 
  This is done by introducing an overcomplete foreground mask that surrounds the 
  vehicle and can be completed by the model to determine nearby vehicles. 
  The code for this research is available at https://github.com/airbluepiano/sensor_foreground.

However, obtaining such datasets on a larger scale poses a problem for various applications, particularly those requiring data with specific characteristics in other domains.  This situation prompts the development of few-shot learning methods in controlled environments and cross-domain knowledge transfer techniques in uncontrolled settings.  In contrast, less attention has been given to scaling issues across uncontrolled environments in the same domain.  This work investigates the possibility of developing a smaller dataset within a domain, capable of supporting training for a wide range of NLP tasks through cross-learning. We further analyzed different pretraining methods and found that fine-tuning the initial set of tasks provides better performance compared to transferring knowledge across diverse tasks.  We have made available a new, smaller dataset called BERTsmall, consisting of annotated instructions and pretrained models for easy evaluation and reproduction of our results.  We have also obtained notable improvements when applying this approach to a larger model and a more extensive dataset, though this leads to increased computational costs.  Our findings support using a small, high-quality domestic dataset for pretraining a limited set of tasks before transferring knowledge for NLP applications in the same domain. black hole horizon in Accretion Disks requires an extremely high sensitivity to long-wavelength magnetic fields. A new method has been developed to measure these fields by analyzing the way they distort the spectrum of reflected X-rays. This technique relies on the precise understanding of how radiation reacts to magnetic fields in the disk. A new theoretical framework has been established to predict the reflection spectra affected by these fields, leading to the creation of a synthetic reference spectrum from a non-magnetic system. By comparing this with data from X-ray observations, a strong signal has been found for the magnitude of the largest-scale magnetic fields, revealing a correlation between magnetic field strength and the mass of the black hole. This discovery has significant implications for the theory of how magnetic fields originate and influence the behavior of accretion disks. As long as the barrier's height remains above a critical threshold, the trajectory will eventually stabilize at a fixed point. However, if the barrier's height drops below this threshold, the trajectory could get stuck in a trapped state. Our analysis shows that the probability of being stuck in a trapped state is analogous to the probability of being captured by a harmonic trap in the random walk's configuration space.   incorporates sparse convolution into annotation tasks by first identifying 
  dense regions in a model and then replacing less efficient sparse regions

  memory accesses by up to 5 times.

  variants.

Despite advances in deep learning, providing training data for labeling extreme events is challenging due to the large quantity of necessary data. This approach was tested using a tropical cyclone dataset from the South China Sea and showed promising results with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, the model performed well when trained on data from a different region, indicating its generality. Additionally, the results confirmed that forecasting extreme events at a longer time frame is more feasible than doing so at a shorter time frame. In contrast to traditional methods, the approach has the advantage of utilizing a large quantity of secondary data such as wind speed, atmospheric pressure, and rainfall.   analysis is often avoided due to the significant computational costs of 
  large-scale simulations. This avoidance can lead to a lack of consideration 
  for input uncertainties in decision-support models, even though these 
  uncertainties can result in suboptimal choices. This paper presents a 
  probabilistic approach to reducing the number of simulations required to 
  accurately determine a model's response to input uncertainties. The method 
  relies on genetic algorithms to identify the most informative simulations, 
  which are then used to construct a probabilistic outcome distribution for 
  the model. This distribution serves as the basis for risk analysis along 
  various dimensions, such as cost and environmental impact. The results of a 
  large-scale forest fire simulation study demonstrate that this method 
  effectively reduces the number of simulations needed by a significant amount 
  without compromising the accuracy of the predicted outcome distribution. 
  Furthermore, this method allows for the characterization of uncertain outcomes 
  along different dimensions and the estimation of the associated risks, which 
  can inform decision-makers about the potential consequences of their choices.

from the solar photosphere, known as DOSIS, was an observing instrument part of the International Space Station. Wearable pulse oximetry devices have become common, but overreliance on these devices alone can lead to misuse and false readings due to their limitations. Consequently, it is essential to complement their use with visual oxygen saturation assessment through the use of the SpO2 finger pulse oximeter. Nevertheless, another method, known as the Rational Approximation of Oxygen Saturation (RAOS), has a more straightforward algorithm and is worth considering. This study compares the readability and calculation methods of both methods. A simple linear regression analysis between the RAOS-estimated oxygen saturation levels and the corresponding values obtained from pulse oximetry readings revealed a strong positive correlation. However, it is crucial to note that the RAOS method may result in an underestimation of oxygen saturation levels, particularly at lower levels. Therefore, this study suggests combining the RAOS method with pulse oximetry readings for an accurate measurement. To that end, a decision support system (DSS) was developed to achieve this goal. The proposed DSS initially employs the RAOS method to estimate oxygen saturation levels based on the color of the fingernails and then makes an adjustment by considering the nail color's limitations. Furthermore, the DSS uses a database of corresponding fingernail colors and oxygen saturation levels to facilitate this calculation. As such, the proposed DSS provides an improved estimation of oxygen saturation levels when compared to the initial RAOS approximation. To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed DSS, a study was conducted with a sample size of 300 participants. The results showed a strong positive correlation between the proposed DSS and pulse oximetry readings. Additionally, the study found that the proposed DSS yields an average absolute error of 2.5% when compared to pulse oximetry readings. To further assess the proposed DSS, a sensing task was designed for healthcare professionals to identify participants with oxygen saturation levels below a certain threshold. The results showed that the proposed DSS yielded a high sensing accuracy of 92% when compared to pulse oximetry readings. Consequently, the proposed DSS has the potential to complement the use of pulse oximetry devices by providing a low-cost, non-invasive method for monitoring oxygen saturation levels through the analysis of fingernail colors. Calculating this delicate balance, which determines the onset of a particular type of $\beta$-decay, is particularly challenging in neutron-rich nuclei. Until now, the starting point for such calculations has been a macroscopic-district theory of a sort that treats the underlying physics in a general manner, with the key parameters derived from experiments and simulations of other types. Utilizing a more fundamental approach based on a microscopically-driven mechanism, this study successfully predicts the likelihood of charged-current neutrino $\beta$-decay across the isospin valley floor that spans from $A=40$ to $A=60$, a region characterized by a complex interplay between the spherical, prolate, and oblate nuclear shapes. This prediction, made possible by a recent microscopically-driven simulation of the nuclear spectrum, reveals that areas with a higher probability of charged-current neutrino $\beta$-decay coincide with those marked by a lack of energy gained from the pairing effect, a phenomenon also reflected in the calculated values of the pairing energy, $\mbox{E}_{\rm pair}$, that drop below the threshold of 1 MeV in certain cases. This threshold, it's worth noting, is correlated with the roll-over of the $\beta$-decay probabilities and could be linked to the roll-over of the $\beta$-decay probabilities from two-body to three-body processes.   that have gained popularity, given their ability to capture complex relationships 
  and linkages among data entities. These repositories have various application 
  domains, including network analysis, machine learning, and information retrieval.
  As the scale and intricacy of stored data grow, inducing models on this data 
  becomes increasingly computationally expensive. To address this challenge, 
  our proposed method develops a novel type of neural network that efficiently 
  learns to generalize from these repositories by leveraging their inherent graphical 
  structure. This new model is capable of inducing highly performing models on 
  a range of tasks, including classification, regression, and semi-supervised 
  learning, while requiring significantly less training data compared to 
  conventional supervised learning. Experimental results demonstrate that this 
  model excels in comparison to alternative neural network architectures, 
  including graph neural networks, multi-layer perceptrons, and reinforcement 
  learning-based models, in various scenarios. The code for this model is 
  publicly available online.  In particular, our method achieves performance 
  comparable to that of supervised learning on large datasets by reducing the 
  required training data by a factor of ten, and successfully induces models 
  on small datasets that achieve performance five times better than that of 
  supervised learning on large datasets. This new model has a significant 
  advantage over existing models in terms of efficiency, as it requires 
  substantially less training data, thereby making it ideally suited for 
  scenarios where large-scale labelled data are difficult to obtain. 
  Furthermore, our method exhibits robustness in scenarios where even a small 
  portion of the knowledge repository holds significant informational value, 
  and exhibits a notable improvement in performance when induced models are 
  transferred to new tasks within the same knowledge repository. This is 
  particularly notable in scenarios where new tasks can be supported at little 
  computational cost. This knowledge can be exploited to streamline the 
  development process for large-scale supervised learning projects. 
  Consequently, our method is an highly efficient model that is capable of 
  generalizing from large knowledge repositories with little supervision. 
  Nonetheless, even with a small amount of supervision, our method exceeds 
  the performance of conventional supervised learning models. 
  Accordingly, our method is an innovative model that induces highly 
  performing models on large knowledge repositories with little supervision. 
  This has numerous practical implications, as developing large-scale supervised 
  learning projects is frequently costly due to the extensive resources 
  required for training.

point-virus transmission rate function have been widely applied in various epidemiological scenarios. However, such tests generally assume knowledge of the precise value of the virus transmission rate, which, in reality, is often estimated with some degree of uncertainty. This study explores the impact of this parameter's uncertainty on the results of Bayesian tests for asymmetry. We used simulated data to model the spread of a pathogen in multiple populations with different transmission rates and tested the symmetry of the point-virus transmission rate function for each scenario. Our findings indicate that even when the virus transmission rate is approximately symmetrical in one of the populations, the corresponding posterior distribution often appears bimodal, greatly increasing the risk of mistakenly interpreting this as genuine asymmetry. Furthermore, when the transmission rates of the different populations vary significantly, the results may suggest asymmetry without providing an accurate representation of the data. We discovered this phenomenon to be particularly prevalent when the point-virus transmission rate function is skewed to the high end. This study highlights the need for cautious interpretation of Bayesian tests for asymmetry in the presence of uncertain virus transmission rates. We also suggest considering a measure of the uncertainty of the point-virus transmission rate function in order to reduce the risk of erroneous conclusions. This research has important implications for the analysis of epidemiological data from multiple settings and emphasizes the importance of thoroughly examining the distribution of the parameters prior to conducting further analysis. This is exemplified through an exploration of the results of Bayesian tests for asymmetry under different assumptions about the distribution of the virus transmission rate. This involves modeling the transmission rate using a beta distribution, which allows for flexible representation of a wide range of distributions, from highly uncertain to well-defined. This leads to an interesting finding that, even when the distribution of the transmission rate is already well-defined, conducting a Bayesian test for asymmetry can still result in the interpretation of a bimodal posterior distribution as genuine asymmetry. This study further explores this risk in relation to the method of estimation used for the transmission rate. This involves modeling the transmission rate using a beta distribution and conducting a comparison of the results obtained using maximum likelihood estimation, logistic regression, and Bayesian estimation. This comparison reveals that the risk of mistakenly interpreting a bimodal posterior distribution as genuine asymmetry increases with the degree of non-uniformity of the prior distribution used for estimation. This is demonstrated through a simulation where the true parameter is symmetrical, and the application of a skewed prior leads to the incorrect conclusion of asymmetry. The "copy problem" with a specific grid as the target and an unlimited supply of identical copies of a different grid is equivalent to finding the minimum number of pieces required to assemble one of these grids.

However, in many real-world applications, trained models may not be accessible due to privacy concerns, licensing issues, or simply because the set of personalized models is too large to store. As such, it's not surprising that models addressing these gaps also have the potential to shed light on the cosmological constant problem. as mobile devices and sensors, large-scale data aggregation tasks are becoming common, posing significant challenges to their implementation.  These challenges are compounded when considering the limited resources of wireless devices.  This paper presents an algorithm for a single node to minimize energy consumption while gathering a comprehensive view of data from other nodes.  The proposed solution involves a node, referred to as the aggregator, that collects summaries from neighboring nodes to build a hierarchical representation of data.  This representation is crucial for supporting complex analysis tasks and enabling the aggregator to make informed decisions about which summaries to gather.  The algorithm optimizes a metric that reflects the quality of gathered summaries in relation to their energy cost.  Experimental results show that the proposed algorithm significantly reduces energy consumption while obtaining comparable results with traditional methods.  The algorithm has practical applications in various domains where data needs to be compressed, such as in big data processing, stream processing, and sensor networks.  An implementation of the algorithm in a mobile application demonstrates its usability.   In this research, we explore the possibility of publishing differentially private data sets while safeguarding the privacy of specific sensitive information outside the main data scope.
  To accomplish this, we utilize a threshold-based approach that protects privacy by incorporating an artificial boundary to differentiate normal and sensitive data points.
  We develop two algorithms to determine whether a point is normal or sensitive based on its similarity to neighboring data points.
  These algorithms can be used to generate differentially private means for normal and sensitive data sets, thereby maintaining the privacy of the latter.
  We demonstrate the efficacy of this threshold-based approach in preserving the privacy of sensitive information by analyzing murder rates among US states, employing a small set of economic indicators as background data. 
  We also examine the impact of this method on the accuracy of published means for normal and sensitive data sets. 
  Our results indicate that economic indicators can predict murder rates with a significant degree of accuracy, though publishing differentially private means reduces this precision. 
  We further develop a framework to understand the trade-off between data privacy and predictive power, utilizing regression models. 
  Our analysis reveals that, in certain cases, publishing differentially private means for sensitive data may actually increase the predictive accuracy compared to using non-private means, though this is likely due to initial low precision in those cases.

hole bounce scenario, specifically focusing on the role of radiation during the bounce phase when the universe was highly distorted. By representing the universe as a polytropic fluid, we applied linear perturbation theory to analyze scalar perturbation dynamics. A key assumption that simplifies the analysis is the neglect of perturbations in the radiation component's energy density. Our results demonstrate that, unlike static universes, radiation plays a significant role in the bounce phase, particularly in influencing the scalar perturbation growth. A crucial factor emerges, which we call the "radiation turn-around time," when the scalar perturbation begins to decay due to radiation. Our analysis indicates that the most abundant primordial black holes are created when the radiation turn-around time aligns with their formation time. This condition leads to a specific relationship between the polytropic index, radiation turn-around time, and the mass spectrum of primordial black holes. We further find that the peak mass of primordial black holes is directly related to the turn-around time and the mass of individual bosons. The interplay between radiation and boson properties during the bounce phase offers an exciting explanation for the possibility of a specific mass spectrum of primordial black holes. This explanation differs from the conventional perspective that attributes this phenomenon to a particular boson mass or a critical density of boson fluctuations. The accuracy of our assumed linear perturbation theory is evaluated, in addition to an assessment of our model's limitations and potential future developments. The methodology employed in this study is also applicable to other cosmological scenarios involving fluid dynamics and phase transitions. The key role of radiation during the bounce phase, coupled with its inherent time scale, positions it as a crucial factor in the emergence of primordial black holes, specifically in relation to the oscillations of unstable boson fields. This finding is reflected in a simple, physically motivated relationship between the mass spectrum of primordial black holes and the properties of the boson field. The interplay between boson field properties, radiation, and the bounce phase has a tangible impact on the emergence of primordial black holes, influencing their formation in a particular mass range. The underlying dynamics of the bosonic instability that gives rise to primordial black holes can be understood through the lens of a universal relationship governed by the scalar perturbation growth, the turn-around time of radiation, and the mass of individual bosons. The analysis conducted in this study is specifically tailored to a scenario where the universe can be represented as a polytropic fluid, but the proposed framework is versatile and applicable to other cosmological settings

gaining insights into strong phase transitions - simple kinetic theory and machine learning-driven training on energetic and structural features - are interconnected. Specifically, a key concept from kinetic theory called the relaxation time can be used to inform the training process, thereby enhancing the prediction of material phenomena by deep learning models. A fundamental relationship between the relaxation time, energetic and structural changes, and free energy differences can be leveraged to this end. By applying this connection, we successfully used a relatively simple kinetic theory to predict the results of complex free energy calculations carried out using machine learning within a model known as the lattice gauge theory. Moreover, we found that the underlying physics of the lattice gauge theory can be understood through an analysis of the kinetic theory-derived drivers of phase transition. We have made our code publicly available on GitHub.  We have demonstrated that machine learning-driven training on kinetic theory-informed features facilitates a deeper understanding of the physical processes governing phase transitions, and this knowledge can be used to improve the performance of free energy calculations. We used a lattice gauge theory model as an example, but this technique is applicable to other challenging problems that involve non-trivial phase transitions and multiple metastable states. We have made our code publicly available on GitHub at the following location: https://github.com/DeepCT98. We have also used a realistic kinetic theory simulation to derive a training set for free energy calculations within the lattice gauge theory model at finite temperature. We have further shown that machine learning-driven predictions of the free energy difference are possible when using a training set based on kinetic theory-informed features, and that this technique is applicable to simulations of different model parameters, system sizes, and temperature values. We have validated our results by conducting a thorough analysis of the metastable states and the cascade of phase transitions that occur within the lattice gauge theory model. We have also used a realistic kinetic theory simulation to inform the training process and predict the results of free energy calculations carried out using machine learning within a model known as the O(3) nonlinear sigma model. We have further shown that machine learning-driven predictions of the free energy difference are possible when using a training set based on kinetic theory-informed features, and that this technique is applicable to simulations of different model parameters, system sizes, and non-linear corrections. We have validated our results by conducting a thorough analysis of the metastable states and the cascade of phase transitions that occur within the lattice gauge theory model. We have also used a realistic kinetic theory simulation to derive a training set for free energy calculations within the lattice gauge theory model at finite temperature.

methods for estimating the population parameters of interest in large-scale surveys that incorporate data from multiple sources. These data sources can be thought of as representing different modes of measurement, such as self-reported information and independently verified data. Each of these data sources has its own set of limitations and potential biases. For example, self-reported data may contain inflationary biases, while independently verified data may be limited in scope. We combine these disparate data sets using weighted averages that prioritize accuracy and relevance, thus producing estimated population parameters that are both statistically reliable and minimally affected by individual data sets' limitations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using historical examples, such as estimating the 1942 mortality rate in Nazi-occupied Amsterdam. We also analyze the sample size requirements and level of precision needed for different estimation methods in relation to the characteristics of the data collected in the survey. We further investigate how the accuracy of these estimates can be improved by utilizing more precise definitions of population parameters or by using regression estimation methods. We emphasize the practical utility of these methods for conducting large-scale surveys that can be utilized for the effective implementation of large-scale intervention programs. We provide a theoretical framework for determining the sample size needed for surveys that utilize indirect measurement, such as self-reported information, and demonstrate how this framework can be applied using real data from an intervention study conducted in South Africa. We also include an exhaustive dataset and the code for the analysis of the examples discussed in the paper. We note that further research is needed into the robust estimation of survival rates and the design of survival studies that utilize indirect measurement. We also highlight potential areas for further research, such as the application of machine learning techniques to survive analysis based on self-reported information. We conclude the paper by stressing the importance of utilizing verification data in conjunction with precise definitions of population parameters or outcomes in order to enhance the validity and efficiency of large-scale survival studies. In this model, initial conditions are kept simple and a thermal equilibrium is assumed, with just one degree of freedom per particle type. Contrary to typical assumptions, we don't let the plasma evolve according to bulk viscosity, instead incorporating a gradient of entropy per unit rapidity to represent nuclear effects within a relativistic fluid dynamics framework. By applying this model to lead-lead collisions at the LHC, we are able to accurately reproduce central particle densities and flow measurements over a wide range of transverse momentum and beam energy. Furthermore, we find that a linear description of the initial state, characterized by a constant entropy gradient, sufficiently captures particle flow measurements and predicts minimal variation in charged particle density with increases in beam energy. Unlike conventional parameter reduction techniques that rely on regularization or filtered methods, our approach leverages the non-convex optimization inherent in neural network training. We show that, due to the stochastic gradient descent algorithm's behavior, optimizing the Euclidean norm of a neuron's weights results in a sparse solution. However, there are cases where the length of a shortest loop equaling the norm does not hold, and such instances are referred to as a norm-discrepancy. The term loop discrepancy was coined to describe the maximum difference between the length of a shortest loop and the norm in a graph. The main contribution of this paper is to introduce new metrics, the maximum loop discrepancy, the average loop discrepancy, and the incidence loop discrepancy, to study the relationship between these metrics and other geometric properties of a graph. The paper goes on to explore specific classes of graphs to identify patterns and provide bounds for these metrics. Furthermore, new inequalities have been established in the paper that connect the maximum/average/total loop discrepancies to other proven and existing metrics. The paper also introduces the concept of a graph's loop radius, which is equivalent to the minimum radius that surrounds the graph without touching any edge, and establishes that it remains discrete from its vertex counterpart, the metric radius, with a gap that can grow infinitely as indicated by a sequence of treelike graphs. The paper further explores the applicability of these metrics to loops of a given length and introduces a grading system for graphs based on their loop discrepancies. The paper also investigates the relationship between the geometric Thomasian discrepancy of a graph and the loop discrepancies, and establishes a ratio between the maximum loop discrepancy and the metric radius for a special class of trees. The paper also provides a lower/upper bound for the average/maximum loop discrepancies of a series of treelike graphs, and the scalar factor can be any real number greater than one. abilities of multilingual machine translation systems compared to their single-language counterparts remains an open research question. One widely accepted theory suggests that low-resource single-language models benefit from the transfer of linguistic knowledge gathered from high-resource translation tasks in multiple languages. However, our research discovered that despite significant training computational costs, these models fail to generalize effectively to isolated low-resource translation tasks. In particular, we found that the knowledge they acquire is primarily practical, consisting of pre- and post-processing techniques rather than genuine linguistic knowledge. As a result, our findings indicate that the generalization advantages of multi-language models are largely a consequence of seamless domain adaptation rather than successful linguistic knowledge transfer. To support this claim, we developed a simple comparison that leverages different translation domains without significant computational costs, and our results confirm that these models readily leverage easy-target domains over harder ones. Our research highlights the importance of distinguishing between true and apparent hard/soft targets, and we believe this terminology provides a clear and useful framework for analyzing the behavior of these models. Our findings also raise concerns about overgeneralization given the smooth domain adaptation abilities of these models, and we believe this is a crucial consideration in evaluating and deploying them in practice. Our research was conducted using a range of small-scale translation tasks, but we have included a large-scale experiment to demonstrate that our findings are scalable. Our research conclusions suggest that while multi-language models do achieve significant generalization gains, this is largely a result of their ability to selectively target easy translation domains rather than a result of successful linguistic knowledge transfer. To address this, we believe that our proposed comparison framework can be utilized to enhance the robustness of these models by penalizing them for shifting to easier targets, and this is a crucial step in ensuring that they generalize effectively to unrelated translation domains. Our research has significant implications for enhancing the robustness of multi-language models with respect to unseen translation domains, and we believe that our proposed comparison framework provides a clear and useful strategy for achieving this. This generalized a similar finding for hyperbolic surfaces by Colding and Minicozzi, and a result for hyperbolic target manifolds with large genus by Miller and Hoffman. The original proof by Iizuka, Nakashima and Yoshida leverages topological insights and slice tests, whereas the present work utilizes conformal structures and uniformization.. 

The underlying idea behind the current approach is the observation that any closed geodesic on a target surface can be expressed as the image of an analytic embedding from a circle into the surface. Furthermore, a key inequality for target surfaces with negative extrinsic curvature is derived, along with an upper bound for the number of closed geodesics within a specific length range. Additionally, a lower bound for the number of closed geodesics on a target surface with positive curvature is obtained, which leads to the conclusion that such surfaces have at least two distinct lengths of closed geodesics.. 

The proposed approach provides a framework for extending this result to target manifolds of higher dimensions, as well as a broader class of surfaces with non-positive curvature, although the precise bounds on the number of geodesics may vary in these cases..
